definitions.definition: Way of working, organising or doing tasks according to a fixed plan, program or set of rules in order to achieve set goals.
Hardware with software embedded in it for a dedicated application, containing at least one programmable computer such as a microcontroller, processor or DSP chip.
Single-chip semiconductor device that is a computer on a chip, but not a complete computer.
Functional computer system on a chip containing a processor, memory and programmable input/output peripherals.
System software that manages computer hardware and software by providing common services among multiple services.
Mid-level language combining high-level features such as functions and modules with low-level features such as good access to hardware through pointers.
Intel's designation for its family of 8051 devices, whose original member is the core for all of them.
Register incremented just before data is stored by a push, call or interrupt and initialised to 07H on reset.
Read-write memory technology that stores information in a small capacitor, which discharges quickly and so must be refreshed frequently.
Read-write memory technology that uses a form of electronic flip-flop to store the information.
Memory form that is write-once, read-many, also called one-time programmable.
16-byte area of data memory that can also be accessed using bit addresses and is used to store bit-sized variables.
Device whose registers and data bus are 8 bits wide, handling 8-bit data quickly and 16-bit or 32-bit data less efficiently.
16-bit counting register that can hold values between 0 and 65535 in decimal.
Hardware mechanism that notifies the processor that an internal or external event, such as timer overflow or serial data arrival, has occurred.
Function written to handle an interrupt, located elsewhere in code memory.
Repeated making and breaking of mechanical switch contacts after the switch is closed or opened, usually lasting under 20 ms.
Internal resistor on a port that pulls the pin up to the microcontroller supply voltage, typically 5V, when the switch is open.
Style well supported by C in which a source file acts as the class, its static data are private members and its functions are member functions.
Header file included in all projects that groups key information about the 8051 device used, such as oscillator frequency and type definitions.
File produced by the compiler manufacturer, linked first in the project header, that makes the ports and other components of the device accessible.
C keyword that provides aliases for data types, so that the aliases can be used in place of the original types.
Header file that pulls together the port access features of a whole project in one place, easing development and maintenance.
Delay created with one of the on-chip timers of the 8051 family, allowing more accurate timing than software loops.
Event that occurs when a 16-bit timer is incremented past its maximum count of 65535.
Special function register holding the timer run-control bits TR0 and TR1 and the external interrupt flags IE0 and IE1.
Special function register that selects the mode of operation of each timer using the M1 and M0 bits, with GATE and counter/timer controls.
Extra, more flexible timer found in devices based on the slightly later 8052 architecture.
Technique that prevents a system from hanging forever when an expected event, such as release of a switch, never occurs.
Timeout built from a loop variable that keeps running until it reaches its maximum value of 65535 and overflows.
Timeout created by using a timer, which allows precise timeout delays to be generated easily.
Software architecture with a series of system states, each calling one or more functions, with rules defining the transitions between states.
System in which the transition between states depends only on the passage of time.
System in which the transition between states, and behaviour in each state, depends on both the passage of time and system inputs.
